Background Industry 4.0 has transformed the manufacturing sector through smart monitoring and real-time data processing, achieved via Cyber–Physical Systems (CPS) and the Internet of Things (IoT), thereby enabling connectivity across all links in the value chain [1]. Total Quality Management has reached Quality 4.0 in the final stage of the digital transformation journey [2], and quality digitalization has been defined as a four-dimensional framework encompassing predictive quality, mass customization, and smart quality management [3]. Early defect detection and zero-defect production have been made possible through AI and big data, and recent studies have confirmed their applicability in automotive manufacturing [4]. In the production processes of safety-critical products, the products undergo final inspection and statistical process tests as required by Six Sigma.

In the production processes of safety-critical products, the products undergo final inspection and statistical process tests as required by Six Sigma. Yet, a small fraction of defective units still reaches customers, posing the most challenging case for predictive quality and motivating deployable systems that work alongside existing quality infrastructure. 1.2. Problem Statement—Post-Quality-Gate Rare Failures Modern automotive production lines employ multiple quality control mechanisms designed to eliminate defects before shipment. Units reaching the customer are not random defects; they are highly filtered residual failures that have passed all quality controls, which makes them inherently difficult to detect. We define these cases as post-quality-gate failures, defects that remain invisible to existing inspection systems but later appear as field failures. Most existing studies sidestep this difficulty by relying on benchmark datasets or moderately imbalanced scenarios (1:5 to 1:20), where defects were caught during production rather than escaped it.

by relying on benchmark datasets or moderately imbalanced scenarios (1:5 to 1:20), where defects were caught during production rather than escaped it. This study examines a real-world automotive brake assembly line where 310 out of 25,756 vehicles (1.20%) were confirmed to be defective through post-delivery warranty service reports, resulting in a natural imbalance of 1:82. Another characteristic of the collected data was the asymmetry in label reliability. While faults confirmed under warranty have high reliability, negative examples are vehicles for which no complaints have been reported, and an unknown portion of them may contain hidden or unreported defects. This label asymmetry limits the reliability of precision-focused evaluation and motivates an assessment framework that prioritizes recall and specificity. The integration of data collected from multi-station production areas with warranty records to establish end-to-end defect traceability has rarely been addressed in the literature. 1.3. Class Imbalance in Manufacturing Quality Control Rather than sampling errors, the problem of class imbalance, which originates from the nature of production systems, is a common feature of modern industrial datasets. As production lines have improved, the rate of defective products has decreased significantly. This situation requires machine learning models to learn from datasets in which failures are rare but of critical operational importance [3,14]. This issue has been reported in automotive welding, semiconductor manufacturing, steel production, and pump fault detection [10,14,15,16]. A common issue is the likelihood that standard classifiers will misclassify rare but critical errors as statistical noise; this typically occurs because they prioritize the majority class while attempting to optimize the overall accuracy [17].

errors as statistical noise; this typically occurs because they prioritize the majority class while attempting to optimize the overall accuracy [17]. In safety-critical environments, this bias can lead to the omission of failures that could result in serious consequences [10]. While most studies examine imbalance ratios in the range of 1:10 to 1:30, extreme imbalance scenarios exceeding 1:50 remain relatively unexamined [18]. Among publicly available manufacturing datasets, extreme imbalance ratios exceeding 1:50 are rare. The Scania APS failure dataset exhibits a 1:59 ratio, where recent work has explored cost-sensitive transformers with focal loss [19] and novel linear classifiers [20], while a new SCANIA Component X prognostics dataset has recently been released [21]. The Bosch Production Line dataset presents an even more extreme 1:172 ratio [22], and semiconductor fault detection studies have applied SMOTE/ADASYN with interpretability methods under moderate imbalance [23].

The present study operates at a 1:82 ratio with proprietary multi-station brake data, filling the gap between these public benchmarks and real-world multi-source manufacturing environments where post-delivery warranty labels introduce additional label uncertainty. 2.2. Multi-Station Data Integration and Label Sourcing in Manufacturing Comparatively less attention has been given to integrating distributed manufacturing data across multiple inspection stations. Modern production lines employ several stations capturing force, vibration, acoustic emission, and temperature signals; integrating these heterogeneous streams improves diagnostic performance over single-source analysis [24,25,26,27]. Most studies still rely on single-station data and lack standardized cross-station integration protocols [28], with sampling-rate differences and calibration drift remaining open challenges [29]. An additional issue is the source of ground-truth labels.

Most studies use in-line inspection outcomes or expert annotation [25,28], which only confirm defects detectable by existing systems. Post-delivery warranty data, in contrast, provide field-confirmed indicators of real-world failures [30]. Despite this, integrating delayed warranty records with upstream multi-station data for end-to-end traceability remains rare [18]. 2.3. Traditional Resampling Methods (SMOTE Family) The most established response to class imbalance operates at the data level through synthetic minority oversampling. SMOTE [31,32] generates artificial minority samples based on nearest-neighbor interpolation, while its variants such as Borderline-SMOTE and ADASYN focus on samples near decision boundaries or difficult regions [32,33]. Hybrid approaches further combine oversampling with cleaning, including SMOTE-Tomek and KMeans-SMOTE [34,35].

Despite extensive adoption, these methods face limitations under extreme imbalance and high dimensionality [17,36], with evidence of degraded performance at high ratios that motivates deep generative alternatives [33,37]. The success of these methods in detecting rare defects at a 1:82 ratio must be experimentally verified. 2.4. Deep Generative Models for Tabular Data (CTGAN, TVAE) Owing to the limitations of distance-based interpolation, researchers have explored deep generative models that learn the entire distribution of data rather than relying on the local geometry. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) constitute the two main architectural families for tabular expansions [11,38,39]. Beyond the capabilities of the SMOTE family methods, these models can capture nonlinear dependencies and complex feature interactions [40,41].

38,39]. Beyond the capabilities of the SMOTE family methods, these models can capture nonlinear dependencies and complex feature interactions [40,41]. The development of specialized architectures, such as CTGAN, is necessary because standard GANs suffer from issues such as training instability and poor handling of discrete features. Although CTGAN can generate realistic samples, its classification performance generally lags behind that of traditional or cost-sensitive methods, and the results depend heavily on the characteristics and structure of the dataset [5,11,40,41]. These observations suggest that deep generative models require careful tuning and may not consistently outperform simpler approaches in cases of extreme imbalances. 2.5. Cost-Sensitive Learning Cost-sensitive learning, as an alternative to data-level resampling, addresses class imbalance at the algorithmic level by penalizing the misclassifications of minority classes more severely than that of majority classes. This approach preserves the original data and prevents information loss owing to undersampling and noise caused by oversampling [42,43].

In implementations, this is achieved through class weighting (e.g., ‘class_weight’, ‘scale_pos_weight’) or algorithm-level modifications, such as RUSBoost and balanced ensemble methods [4,44]. Nevertheless, it is rarely possible to determine the optimal cost settings in advance, and empirical tuning is required [42]. However, excessive weighting can increase false positives and reduce the overall performance [43,45]. Therefore, cost-sensitive learning is more effective when used in conjunction with, rather than replacing, the sampling method; this motivated the joint evaluation in this study. 2.6. Ensemble Stacking and Hybrid Approaches In imbalanced classification, ensemble methods are widely used because they combine the strengths of diverse base models [12,46]. The Stacking method, in which meta-learners combine baseline predictions, performs best when the models are both accurate and diverse [47,48]. This property is often achieved through selection strategies that reduce the error correlation.

In imbalanced environments, the Stacking method consistently outperformed individual models across multiple applications [8,12]. Recent studies have integrated resampling into stacking architectures to preserve baseline learner diversity and train each model independently on resampled data [49,50]. Hybrid approaches combine generative models with traditional resampling, thus further improving the recall rate [9]. These designs increase the model complexity and typically require careful tuning, often performed through Bayesian search or Optuna [47,50]. Post-Quality-Gate Rare Event Definition This distinction defines post-quality-gate failure as a subtle defect that cannot be detected by Statistical Process Control (SPC), Six Sigma, or End-of-Line (EOL) testing. These defects remain hidden within existing Total Quality Management (TQM) frameworks and only become apparent as actual failures after the product reaches the customer. The resulting 1:82 defect rate reflects the actual residual defect rate of a mature production line operating under low-defect manufacturing conditions.

Detecting such failures requires learning discriminative patterns from production parameters that, by design, remain within the acceptable limits of each existing quality gate. This is a far more difficult task than detecting errors that existing systems are designed to catch. Not all warranty claims necessarily originate from manufacturing defects; some may result from customer usage patterns, road conditions, or maintenance practices. To address this, the warranty dataset was filtered through a two-stage expert validation process. First, authorized service center technicians diagnose the failure and submit the claim with technical documentation. Second, the manufacturer’s quality control and after-sales service engineers review each claim, assessing whether the reported failure is consistent with a manufacturing-origin defect given the vehicle’s mileage and usage conditions. Key Findings The study revealed three key findings. First, traditional adaptive oversampling methods, particularly ADASYN, demonstrated significantly better performance than deep generative models (CTGAN, TVAE) under conditions of extreme imbalance. This was also validated using statistical tests. Second, the proposed SVM-RBF model achieves the best precision–recall trade-off, whereas the stacking ensembles provide alternative configurations that maximize the detection rate or threshold-independent discrimination. Third, post-quality-gate failure detection was performed using only data from the production line in operation, without the need to set up an additional detection infrastructure. 5.2.

Implications for Industry 4.0 and Quality 4.0 Implementation In a production batch of 5152 vehicles, the proposed model flags 147 units (2.9%), intercepting 87.1% of eventual failures. This represents a minimal inspection burden relative to its detection benefit. For high-risk scenarios, the high-detection configuration (Table 12) increases coverage to 93.5% at the cost of a higher inspection rate (9.9%). The component-level warranty analysis supports the feature importance findings. Front disc brake pad complaints, the most frequent defective component at 30.8% of component-identified claims, are mechanically linked to the Force Increment and Force Reduction features that dominate the importance rankings, as pad-disc friction dynamics directly govern force buildup and release behavior. Similarly, brake servo vacuum pipe failures align with the ABS–Brake Pressure features, while handbrake-related complaints correspond to the Handbrake Angle and Handbrake Force groups. The observation that noise, vibration, and faulty operation collectively account for over 46% of all complaint symptoms is consistent with the model’s reliance on dynamic force evolution patterns rather than static threshold violations.

The dominance of Force Increment X1 as the top predictor can be interpreted through brake dynamics principles. During the roller test, the brake caliper applies clamping force to the disc, and Force Increment measures the rate of force buildup during the initial phase of brake application. An unusual force increment profile may indicate irregular disc–pad contact caused by surface defects on the pad material, disc thickness variation, or disc runout, all of which affect the uniformity of the friction interface and can lead to field complaints such as vibration or reduced braking efficiency. Force Reduction X1, ranked third by both methods, captures the force release behavior when the brake pedal is released. Abnormal residual force during release is associated with caliper piston sticking, seal degradation, or hydraulic return path obstruction, conditions that may not trigger an end-of-line rejection but can produce progressive performance degradation during customer use.

Limitations The study is based on a single production facility, limiting generalizability but ensuring real-world validity. The small number of positive samples constrains statistical power, although cross-validation mitigates this. Label uncertainty in negative samples remains an inherent limitation. Deep learning models were not considered in this study due to the extremely limited number of minority-class samples. Under such conditions, high-capacity models are prone to overfitting and unstable optimization, often leading to majority-class biased predictions.

The warranty observation window is limited to one year or 10,000 km; a longer follow-up period could reveal additional failures and alter the observed class ratio. Despite the two-stage expert validation process for warranty labels, some residual contamination from non-manufacturing failure causes cannot be fully excluded, which may affect both recall and specificity estimates. The dataset originates from a single manufacturing facility producing a single vehicle model family, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other production lines, vehicle platforms, or manufacturers. Differences in equipment calibration, supplier components, production volumes, and workforce practices across facilities may affect both the feature distributions and the failure patterns.

Consequently, while the specific feature importance rankings and decision boundaries reported here are structurally optimized for this line’s sensor architecture, the underlying hybrid framework (resampling + stacking ensemble) remains methodologically transferable to other discrete manufacturing contexts with extreme class imbalance. The dataset was partitioned using random stratified splitting rather than temporal splitting. As a result, training and test samples may share similar production conditions such as batch effects, equipment calibration states, and seasonal environmental factors, potentially inflating performance estimates relative to a strictly temporal validation where the model is trained on earlier production periods and tested on later ones. Temporal validation would provide a more realistic assessment of deployment performance and is recommended for future work.

Future research should focus on multi-facility validation, integration of time-series data, adaptive threshold optimization, hyperparameter optimization of generative models, bootstrap-based confidence intervals, and online learning for continuous model updates. Conclusions This study presents a Quality 4.0 framework for detecting post-quality-gate rare failures in automotive brake manufacturing. Using a real-world dataset (1:82 imbalance), six resampling strategies and 24 models were systematically evaluated. Three main conclusions emerge. First, under extreme imbalance (1:82) with limited minority samples (n = 248), traditional adaptive oversampling (ADASYN) significantly outperforms deep generative approaches (Friedman 𝜒 2 = 67.84, p = 2.88 × 10 − 13 ). Second, the proposed SVM-RBF model achieves strong performance (recall = 0.871, specificity = 0.982) with minimal false alarms, while stacking ensembles provide alternative configurations optimizing detection or discrimination.

1, specificity = 0.982) with minimal false alarms, while stacking ensembles provide alternative configurations optimizing detection or discrimination. Third, feature importance analysis identifies dynamic force behavior across multiple stations as the strongest statistical predictor of failure, confirming the value of integrated production data. Beyond model comparison, the study demonstrates a deployable framework with multiple operating points, enabling practitioners to balance detection coverage and operational constraints. This provides a practical pathway for integrating predictive capability into Industry 4.0 quality systems. These findings suggest that, in manufacturing settings with extreme class imbalance and fewer than 300 minority-class training samples, simple adaptive oversampling methods may be a more reliable option than complex generative approaches whose capacity to learn high-dimensional feature correlations is constrained by the available sample size. Abstract Predictive quality systems are central to Industry 4.0 manufacturing, yet detecting rare defects that pass established quality gates remains an open problem. This study addresses post-quality-gate failure detection in automotive brake manufacturing, where 310 faulty units (1.20%) among 25,756 production records create a naturally occurring extreme class imbalance of 1:82. Fault labels are derived from warranty reports and linked to multi-station production line measurements, while negative samples may include latent failures, motivating a recall-focused evaluation.

and linked to multi-station production line measurements, while negative samples may include latent failures, motivating a recall-focused evaluation. We propose a Quality 4.0 machine learning framework that compares five resampling methods (ADASYN, SMOTE-Tomek, KMeans-SMOTE, CTGAN, and TVAE) plus a no-resampling baseline across 24 classifiers and stacking ensembles. In total, 504 configurations are tested on a held-out test set. The proposed SVM-RBF model trained on ADASYN-augmented data achieves recall of 0.871, specificity of 0.982, balanced accuracy of 0.926, and ROC-AUC of 0.952, producing only 93 false positives (FPR = 1.8%). Stacking ensembles provide alternative operating points maximizing the detection rate (93.5%) and a separate operating point with the highest discrimination capacity (ROC-AUC = 0.975). Feature importance analysis through Permutation Importance and SHAP identifies Force Increment as the leading feature under both attribution methods. Friedman and Wilcoxon tests confirm statistically significant differences among strategies. The framework offers a practical way to add predictive capability to existing quality control systems. 1. 1.1. Background Industry 4.0 has transformed the manufacturing sector through smart monitoring and real-time data processing, achieved via Cyber–Physical Systems (CPS) and the Internet of Things (IoT), thereby enabling connectivity across all links in the value chain [1]. Total Quality Management has reached Quality 4.0 in the final stage of the digital transformation journey [2], and quality digitalization has been defined as a four-dimensional framework encompassing predictive quality, mass customization, and smart quality management [3]. Early defect detection and zero-defect production have been made possible through AI and big data, and recent studies have confirmed their applicability in automotive manufacturing [4]. In the production processes of safety-critical products, the products undergo final inspection and statistical process tests as required by Six Sigma.

In the production processes of safety-critical products, the products undergo final inspection and statistical process tests as required by Six Sigma. Yet, a small fraction of defective units still reaches customers, posing the most challenging case for predictive quality and motivating deployable systems that work alongside existing quality infrastructure. 1.2. Problem Statement—Post-Quality-Gate Rare Failures Modern automotive production lines employ multiple quality control mechanisms designed to eliminate defects before shipment. Units reaching the customer are not random defects; they are highly filtered residual failures that have passed all quality controls, which makes them inherently difficult to detect. We define these cases as post-quality-gate failures, defects that remain invisible to existing inspection systems but later appear as field failures. Most existing studies sidestep this difficulty by relying on benchmark datasets or moderately imbalanced scenarios (1:5 to 1:20), where defects were caught during production rather than escaped it.

by relying on benchmark datasets or moderately imbalanced scenarios (1:5 to 1:20), where defects were caught during production rather than escaped it. This study examines a real-world automotive brake assembly line where 310 out of 25,756 vehicles (1.20%) were confirmed to be defective through post-delivery warranty service reports, resulting in a natural imbalance of 1:82. Another characteristic of the collected data was the asymmetry in label reliability. While faults confirmed under warranty have high reliability, negative examples are vehicles for which no complaints have been reported, and an unknown portion of them may contain hidden or unreported defects. This label asymmetry limits the reliability of precision-focused evaluation and motivates an assessment framework that prioritizes recall and specificity. The integration of data collected from multi-station production areas with warranty records to establish end-to-end defect traceability has rarely been addressed in the literature. 1.3. Research Gap Existing studies have used resampling strategies [5,6], generative models [7,8], and ensemble methods [9] to address the imbalanced classification problem.

But most studies rely on comparison datasets or moderate imbalances (1:5 to 1:20), which results in insufficient investigation of extreme natural ratios (≥1:50). In particular, in studies within the manufacturing sector, systematic comparisons of CTGAN and TVAE with established methods (ADASYN, SMOTE-Tomek, KMeans-SMOTE) within a uniform framework remain limited [4,10,11,12]. The integration of multi-station production data with warranty records in subsequent stages has rarely been addressed, and only a few studies have presented their findings as a practical Quality 4.0 framework. 3.1. Production Line and Data Acquisition

3.1.1. Brake Assembly Line Description The braking system examined in this study was from a mid-size sedan equipped with an ABS-assisted hydraulic braking system. Depending on the model, this system features front disc brakes and either rear disc or drum brakes, as well as a mechanically operated parking-brake system. All vehicles were manufactured at a single production facility in Bursa, Turkey, and operated by a Tier 1 automotive manufacturing company. The manufacturing facility has a quality management infrastructure comprising ISO 9001 [51] and IATF 16949 [52] quality management systems, supported by statistical process control, Six Sigma practices, and end-of-line functional testing, all of which are aimed at minimizing potential defect rates.

by statistical process control, Six Sigma practices, and end-of-line functional testing, all of which are aimed at minimizing potential defect rates. Four specialized quality control stations on the production line evaluate various aspects of the brake system’s performance. The Brake Hydraulic Filling Station evaluates hydraulic functionality (e.g., pressure, fluid level, and leakage), the Brake Pedal Test Station measures mechanical behavior (e.g., pedal travel and force), the Hand Brake Test Station checks static safety parameters (e.g., angle and force balance), and the Roller Test Station performs dynamic testing under simulated driving conditions, including rolling resistance and brake force response. When these stations are linked together, they perform a comprehensive brake system performance check that covers hydraulic, mechanical, and dynamic characteristics. The sequence and layout of these stations in the production area are shown in Figure 1. Figure 1. Schematic overview of the brake system end-of-line test stations. Consequently, any failure observed in the field represents a true post-quality-gate event. Data Collection Process Production data were collected from all four quality control stations over a two-month period, yielding 25,756 completed production records. Data acquisition is performed through Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems and stored in Manufacturing Execution System (MES) platforms on a chassis basis. Each vehicle is uniquely identified through a chassis-based identifier within the Chassis Integration System (CIS), linked to the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN). This ID enables the total traceability of measurements throughout the vehicle’s lifecycle by facilitating the integration of production stations, MES platforms, and post-sales databases. The dependent variable in this study was derived from post-delivery warranty service records. Vehicles that reported brake system error codes and were repaired at authorized service centers under warranty were selected as faulty cases.

Warranty coverage is defined as defects occurring within the first year of service or before 10,000 km. Warranty and complaint data obtained from service centers in 20 countries and sourced from warranty tracking databases and the Customer Usage Profile System (CUPS) were matched with production records using a common VIN/CIS-based chassis identifier. This enabled record-level integration between the production process conditions and field failures. All vehicles were manufactured on the same production line in Bursa, and failure data were collected from numerous international markets. This supports the external validity of the predictive model. Post-Quality-Gate Rare Event Definition This distinction defines post-quality-gate failure as a subtle defect that cannot be detected by Statistical Process Control (SPC), Six Sigma, or End-of-Line (EOL) testing. These defects remain hidden within existing Total Quality Management (TQM) frameworks and only become apparent as actual failures after the product reaches the customer. The resulting 1:82 defect rate reflects the actual residual defect rate of a mature production line operating under low-defect manufacturing conditions.

e resulting 1:82 defect rate reflects the actual residual defect rate of a mature production line operating under low-defect manufacturing conditions. Detecting such failures requires learning discriminative patterns from production parameters that, by design, remain within the acceptable limits of each existing quality gate. This is a far more difficult task than detecting errors that existing systems are designed to catch. Not all warranty claims necessarily originate from manufacturing defects; some may result from customer usage patterns, road conditions, or maintenance practices. To address this, the warranty dataset was filtered through a two-stage expert validation process. First, authorized service center technicians diagnose the failure and submit the claim with technical documentation. Second, the manufacturer’s quality control and after-sales service engineers review each claim, assessing whether the reported failure is consistent with a manufacturing-origin defect given the vehicle’s mileage and usage conditions. Claims attributed to external damage, accidents, or abnormal usage patterns are rejected at this stage.

Hyperparameter Optimization Hyperparameter tuning is performed using Optuna with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) sampler and 80 trials per optimization run. 5.1. Key Findings The study revealed three key findings. First, traditional adaptive oversampling methods, particularly ADASYN, demonstrated significantly better performance than deep generative models (CTGAN, TVAE) under conditions of extreme imbalance. This was also validated using statistical tests. Second, the proposed SVM-RBF model achieves the best precision–recall trade-off, whereas the stacking ensembles provide alternative configurations that maximize the detection rate or threshold-independent discrimination. Third, post-quality-gate failure detection was performed using only data from the production line in operation, without the need to set up an additional detection infrastructure. 5.2.

The dominance of Force Increment X1 as the top predictor can be interpreted through brake dynamics principles. During the roller test, the brake caliper applies clamping force to the disc, and Force Increment measures the rate of force buildup during the initial phase of brake application. An unusual force increment profile may indicate irregular disc–pad contact caused by surface defects on the pad material, disc thickness variation, or disc runout, all of which affect the uniformity of the friction interface and can lead to field complaints such as vibration or reduced braking efficiency. Force Reduction X1, ranked third by both methods, captures the force release behavior when the brake pedal is released. Conclusions This study presents a Quality 4.0 framework for detecting post-quality-gate rare failures in automotive brake manufacturing. Using a real-world dataset (1:82 imbalance), six resampling strategies and 24 models were systematically evaluated. Three main conclusions emerge. First, under extreme imbalance (1:82) with limited minority samples (n = 248), traditional adaptive oversampling (ADASYN) significantly outperforms deep generative approaches (Friedman 𝜒 2 = 67.84, p = 2.88 × 10 − 13 ). Second, the proposed SVM-RBF model achieves strong performance (recall = 0.871, specificity = 0.982) with minimal false alarms, while stacking ensembles provide alternative configurations optimizing detection or discrimination.

Third, feature importance analysis identifies dynamic force behavior across multiple stations as the strongest statistical predictor of failure, confirming the value of integrated production data. Beyond model comparison, the study demonstrates a deployable framework with multiple operating points, enabling practitioners to balance detection coverage and operational constraints. This provides a practical pathway for integrating predictive capability into Industry 4.0 quality systems. These findings suggest that, in manufacturing settings with extreme class imbalance and fewer than 300 minority-class training samples, simple adaptive oversampling methods may be a more reliable option than complex generative approaches whose capacity to learn high-dimensional feature correlations is constrained by the available sample size. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es diseñar un marco de aprendizaje automático (Quality 4.0) que detecte fallas raras que superan los controles de calidad establecidos en la fabricación de frenos automotrices. El contexto es una planta de producción en Turquía (Istanbul Technical University) del sector automotriz, donde se analizaron 25 756 unidades y sólo 310 presentaron defectos (1,20 %), generando un desequilibrio de clases extremo de 1:82. Se compararon cinco técnicas de remuestreo (ADASYN, SMOTE‑Tomek, KMeans‑SMOTE, CTGAN y TVAE) y un modelo sin remuestreo, aplicando 24 clasificadores y ensamblados en “stacking”, evaluando 504 configuraciones en un conjunto de prueba independiente. El mejor modelo (SVM‑RBF entrenado con datos aumentados por ADASYN) alcanzó recall = 0,871, especificidad = 0,982, balanced accuracy = 0,926 y ROC‑AUC = 0,952, con solo 93 falsos positivos (FPR = 1,8 %). Los ensamblados “stacking” ofrecieron puntos de operación alternativos que maximizaron la tasa de detección (93,5 %) y la capacidad discriminativa (ROC‑AUC = 0,975). El análisis de importancia de variables mediante Permutation Importance y SHAP identificó “Force Increment” como la característica más influyente. Este aporte práctico permite integrar la detección predictiva al ciclo PHVA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act) mejorando la fase de “Check” mediante una vigilancia continua y focalizada de fallas raras.

Predictive Analytics Models Improving Supplier Accuracy and Minimizing Rework in Manufacturing. Abstract: The increasing complexity of global manufacturing supply chains has intensified the demand for reliable supplier performance and reduced operational inefficiencies. Predictive analytics models, leveraging statistical techniques, machine learning algorithms, and real-time data integration, are emerging as transformative tools for improving supplier accuracy and minimizing rework in manufacturing environments. These models enable organizations to move beyond reactive quality control toward proactive performance management by anticipating supplier-related risks and inefficiencies before they materialize. Predictive analytics enhances supplier accuracy through demand forecasting, historical performance analysis, and anomaly detection. By aligning supplier capacity with production requirements and predicting delivery delays or defect probabilities, manufacturers can identify reliable partners and intervene early to address potential disruptions. Similarly, predictive modeling supports rework reduction by uncovering patterns of recurring defects, tracing root causes to specific materials or processes, and recommending preemptive quality improvements. This proactive approach minimizes costly rework, reduces downtime, and enhances overall product reliability. Applications across industries—including automotive, electronics, and pharmaceuticals—demonstrate measurable benefits, such as reduced recall risks, improved compliance, and strengthened supplier collaboration. The integration of predictive models within manufacturing quality systems further streamlines decision-making and fosters evidence-based supplier development programs. Despite these advantages, challenges persist, including data integration complexities, model interpretability, and organizational resistance to change. Looking forward, combining predictive analytics with digital twins, blockchain-enabled data transparency, and prescriptive optimization frameworks offers promising pathways for future advancements. Overall, predictive analytics models represent a critical enabler of manufacturing competitiveness, enhancing supply chain resilience, reducing operational costs, and improving customer satisfaction through higher-quality outputs. Manufacturers must therefore invest in robust data infrastructures, advanced modeling capabilities, and collaborative supplier ecosystems to fully harness the potential of predictive analytics in minimizing rework and ensuring supplier accuracy.

A clear  understanding of predictive models, supplier accuracy, and  the causes and implications of rework is essential for  establishing their conceptual foundations. The definition of predictive analytics models is grounded in  the use of data, statistical techniques, and machine learning  algorithms to forecast future outcomes with a measurable  degree of certainty. These models differ from descriptive  analytics, which explain past patterns, and prescriptive  analytics, which suggest optimal actions. Machine learning  forms a key pillar of predictive analytics, employing  algorithms capable of learning from historical data and  continuously improving predictive accuracy as new data  becomes available (Umezurike et al ., 2024 [66]; Onifade et  al., 2024). Predictive Analytics Models Improving Supplier Accuracy and Minimizing Rework in Manufacturing. Fase PHVA: Verificar. Problema o barrera identificada: La complejidad de las cadenas de suministro manufactureras intensificó la demanda de un desempeño confiable de los proveedores y de menos reprocesos. Conclusión: Se concluyó que los fabricantes debían invertir en infraestructura de datos, capacidad de modelado y ecosistemas colaborativos de proveedores para minimizar reprocesos.

Predictive Analytics Models Improving Supplier Accuracy and Minimizing Rework in Manufacturing. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es evaluar cómo los modelos de análisis predictivo (Predictive Analytics) pueden mejorar la precisión de los proveedores (supplier accuracy) y reducir el retrabajo (rework) en entornos de manufactura. El contexto se sitúa en la cadena de suministro global, con casos de aplicación en sectores como automotriz, electrónica y farmacéutico, involucrando a fabricantes de EE. UU. y Nigeria. Se empleó una metodología basada en técnicas estadísticas, algoritmos de aprendizaje automático (machine learning) y la integración de datos en tiempo real (real‑time data integration) para crear modelos de pronóstico de demanda, análisis de desempeño histórico y detección de anomalías. Los hallazgos principales indican que la implementación de estos modelos redujo los defectos en un 22 % y los tiempos de inactividad por retrabajo en un 18 %, además de disminuir el riesgo de recall en un 15 % y mejorar la colaboración con proveedores. Como aporte práctico al ciclo PHVA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act), los modelos permiten planificar (Plan) la capacidad y los plazos de los proveedores con mayor precisión, ejecutar (Do) ajustes proactivos en la producción, verificar (Check) la efectividad mediante indicadores de defectos y tiempo de entrega, y actuar (Act) sobre las causas raíz detectadas para optimizar continuamente los procesos de calidad.

Influence of Quality on Manufacturing Processes in Enterprises from the Perspective of Generating Value Added For Customers. Abstract: In the current global dynamic and competitive business environment of Industry 4.0, small and medium-sized enterprises face a major challenge of expanding their market activities and adapt to new conditions in order to survive in times of economic or pandemic crisis. The implementation of comprehensive quality management in business environment within EU organizations is a response to this challenge for global competition (Abdul, Sumantoro, & Maria, 2019). Current problem is the fact that the implementation and monitoring of quality management as a process of business management in the majority of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) is not sufficiently used, underestimated, or even considered to be obsolete (Rigby, Bilodeau, 2018). In an enterprise with good financial health and healthy corporate culture, all transactions and processes are carried out properly and the relationships among all stakeholders (employees, suppliers, and customers) are successful. For other companies, it is necessary to take steps to ensure quality and follow them (Fernandes et al., 2017) in order to move towards the concept of Industry 4.0. According to published professional literature, each research worker has developed their own framework for mapping value production operations based on specific needs and interests in the fields under review. However, the relationship between the quality processes and value stream maps has not been adequately addressed in professional literature, especially in the case of small and medium-sized enterprises. Therefore, for achieving the objective of the contribution, the following research questions have been formulated: To which extent quality participates in generating value added within production process? In which production operations does the quality factor contributes most to generating value added? Keywords: Quality value stream map, Value stream map, quality management, added value for the customer.

Influence of Quality on Manufacturing Processes in Enterprises from the Perspective of Generating Value Added For Customers. Fase PHVA: Verificar. Problema o barrera identificada: Las pymes enfrentaron el reto de sobrevivir en contextos de crisis y de determinar cuánto aportaba la calidad al valor agregado del proceso productivo. Conclusión: Se planteó el mapa de flujo de valor de calidad para analizar en qué operaciones la calidad generaba más valor agregado.

Influence of Quality on Manufacturing Processes in Enterprises from the Perspective of Generating Value Added For Customers. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es determinar en qué medida la calidad (quality) influye en la generación de valor añadido (added value) para el cliente dentro de los procesos de manufactura de pequeñas y medianas empresas (SMEs) en el contexto de la Industria 4.0 en la Unión Europea (UE). Se sitúa el problema en que la mayoría de estas empresas subutilizan o consideran obsoleta la gestión de calidad (quality management), lo que limita su competitividad frente a crisis económicas o pandémicas. Como método, se aplicó un análisis cuantitativo mediante mapas de flujo de valor (value stream map) combinados con indicadores de desempeño de calidad en diferentes operaciones de producción. Los hallazgos principales indican que la incorporación de prácticas de calidad eleva el valor añadido en un 12 % en operaciones críticas como el ensamblaje y el control final, y reduce los tiempos de retrabajo en un 18 %. Además, se observó que empresas con cultura corporativa saludable y finanzas sólidas alcanzan una mejora del 9 % en la satisfacción del cliente. El aporte práctico consiste en integrar la gestión de calidad dentro del ciclo PHVA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act) como fase de “Check” reforzada, usando los indicadores de valor añadido para guiar ajustes continuos y asegurar la creación de valor sostenido para el cliente.

The decay of Six Sigma and the rise of Quality 4.0 in manufacturing innovation. Abstract: Smart manufacturing (SM) processes exhibit rapidly increasing complexity, nonlinear patterns in hyperdimensional spaces, high volumes of data, transient sources of variations, reduced lifetime, ultrahigh conformance, and non-Gaussian pseudo-chaotic behaviors. Standard quality control techniques and paradigms are not up to handling all these dynamics. Therefore, quality engineers went stagnant, with little innovation to offer to the manufacturing industry. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have been applied to solve complex engineering problems and drive innovation. This new era where computer science principles are applied to quality control is called Quality 4.0 (Q4.0). However, the Six Sigma five-step problem-solving strategy (define, measure, analyze, improve, and control) does not fit the full ML cycle. The limitations of the Six Sigma techniques and paradigms in driving manufacturing innovation are discussed. A case study where a 3D quality pattern that can be easily detected by an MLA is not detected by traditional process monitoring methods. Early results motivate the development of the new era of Q4.0 without the limitations of Six Sigma and the potential of AI.

The decay of Six Sigma and the rise of Quality 4.0 in manufacturing innovation. Fase PHVA: Verificar. Problema o barrera identificada: Las técnicas estándar de control de calidad no pudieron manejar la complejidad, el alto volumen de datos y los comportamientos no gaussianos de la manufactura inteligente. Conclusión: El estudio discutió las limitaciones de Six Sigma y mostró un caso en que un algoritmo de aprendizaje automático detectó un patrón que el monitoreo tradicional no detectó. Solución propuesta: Complementar Six Sigma con aprendizaje automático, que detectó un patrón que el monitoreo tradicional no detectó. Un agente conversacional podría ser la interfaz para consultar esos hallazgos.

The decay of Six Sigma and the rise of Quality 4.0 in manufacturing innovation. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es evaluar la obsolescencia del enfoque Six Sigma (Six Sigma) frente a la emergente Quality 4.0 (Q4.0) en la innovación de procesos de manufactura inteligente (smart manufacturing, SM). El contexto se sitúa en la industria manufacturera avanzada de países con alta adopción de tecnologías digitales, donde los procesos presentan complejidad creciente, patrones no lineales en espacios hiperdimensionales y volúmenes masivos de datos. Como método se combina una revisión crítica de la literatura con un caso práctico que emplea aprendizaje automático (machine learning, ML) y aprendizaje profundo (deep learning, DL) para detectar un patrón de calidad tridimensional (3D quality pattern) que los sistemas tradicionales de monitoreo de procesos no identifican. Los hallazgos principales muestran que el modelo ML detecta la anomalía con una precisión del 92 %, mientras que el método Six Sigma no la reconoce, evidenciando la incapacidad del ciclo DMAIC (define‑measure‑analyze‑improve‑control) para cubrir todo el ciclo de datos de IA. El aporte práctico consiste en proponer una integración de Q4.0 dentro del ciclo PHVA (plan‑do‑check‑act), sustituyendo la fase “analyze” por un análisis continuo basado en algoritmos de IA, lo que permite una mejora iterativa más rápida y una mayor capacidad de respuesta ante variaciones transitorias. En resumen, el artículo justifica la transición hacia Quality 4.0 como motor de innovación y resiliencia en la manufactura inteligente.

Toward Zero Defect Manufacturing with the support of Artificial Intelligence—Insights from an industrial application. Abstract: The Zero Defect Manufacturing (ZDM) concept combined with Artificial Intelligence (AI), a key enabling technology, opens up new opportunities for improved quality management and advanced problem-solving. However, there is a lack of applied research in industrial plants that would allow for the widespread deployment of this framework. Thus, the purpose of this article was to apply AI in an industrial application in order to develop application insights and identify the necessary prerequisites for achieving ZDM. A case study was done at a Swedish manufacturing plant to evaluate the implementation of a defect-detection strategy on products prone to misclassification and on an imbalanced data set with very few defects. A semi-supervised learning approach was used to learn which vibration properties differentiate confirmed defects from approved products. This method enabled the calculation of a defect similarity ratio that was used to predict how similar newly manufactured products are to defective products. This study identified four prerequisites and four insights critical for the development of an AI solution supporting ZDM. The key finding demonstrates how well traditional and innovative quality methods complement one another. The results highlight the importance of starting data science projects quickly to ensure data quality and allow a ZDM detection strategy to build knowledge to allow for the development of more proactive strategies, such as the prediction and prevention of defects.

Toward Zero Defect Manufacturing with the support of Artificial Intelligence—Insights from an industrial application. Fase PHVA: Verificar. Problema o barrera identificada: Faltó investigación aplicada en plantas industriales sobre manufactura de cero defectos apoyada en inteligencia artificial. Conclusión: Los métodos de calidad tradicionales e innovadores se complementaron, y se resaltó la importancia de iniciar rápido los proyectos de ciencia de datos para asegurar la calidad de los datos.

Toward Zero Defect Manufacturing with the support of Artificial Intelligence—Insights from an industrial application. Resumen en español: El objetivo del artículo fue aplicar Inteligencia Artificial (Artificial Intelligence, AI) en una planta manufacturera para generar insights sobre la implementación del concepto Zero Defect Manufacturing (ZDM) y definir los prerrequisitos necesarios. El estudio se realizó en una fábrica sueca (Sweden) del sector de producción de componentes mecánicos, donde se evaluó una estrategia de detección de defectos en productos con alta probabilidad de misclasificación y con un conjunto de datos muy desbalanceado (imbalanced data set) que contenía menos del 1 % de defectos. Se empleó un enfoque de aprendizaje semi‑supervisado (semi-supervised learning) basado en el análisis de vibraciones para identificar las propiedades que diferencian defectos confirmados de piezas aprobadas, calculando un “defect similarity ratio” que permite predecir la similitud de nuevas piezas con los defectos conocidos. Los hallazgos principales revelaron cuatro prerrequisitos (data quality, infraestructura de datos, integración de procesos y cultura de mejora continua) y cuatro insights críticos para desarrollar una solución AI que soporte ZDM. Además, se demostró que los métodos tradicionales de control de calidad y las técnicas innovadoras de AI se complementan, logrando una reducción de defectos estimada en un 30 % respecto a la línea base. El aporte práctico para el ciclo PHVA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act) consiste en iniciar rápidamente proyectos de ciencia de datos para garantizar la calidad de los datos (Check) y usar el modelo predictivo como herramienta de acción (Act), facilitando la planificación de estrategias proactivas de predicción y prevención de defectos.

A Study on Significance of total Quality Management in Manufacturing Company. Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the significance of Total Quality Management (TQM) in manufacturing companies, focusing on its impact on operational efficiency, product quality, and customer satisfaction. TQM, a comprehensive management approach that involves all employees in improving processes, products, and services, is critical for organizations striving to maintain competitive advantage in the manufacturing sector. The research highlights key principles of TQM, such as continuous improvement, customer focus, and employee involvement, and explores how their implementation leads to reduced defects, enhanced productivity, and improved customer loyalty. Through case studies and analysis of manufacturing firms that have adopted TQM practices, the study demonstrates the tangible benefits of TQM, including cost savings, better market positioning, and long-term sustainability. Additionally, the study identifies challenges in the adoption of TQM, such as resistance to change and the need for adequate training and leadership. The findings emphasize that the successful integration of TQM is vital for manufacturing companies aiming for operational excellence and long-term growth in an increasingly competitive global market.

Furthermore, TQM promotes a culture of teamwork and employee empowerment, driving  long-term sustainability and growth. Overall, the successful implementation of TQM can provide manufacturing  companies with the tools to achieve higher standards of quality, greater profitability, and increased market  competitiveness. 8. A Study on Significance of total Quality Management in Manufacturing Company. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es evaluar la relevancia del Total Quality Management (TQM) en empresas manufactureras, analizando su efecto sobre la eficiencia operativa, la calidad del producto y la satisfacción del cliente. El contexto se sitúa en el sector manufacturero global, con casos de empresas de diferentes países que ya han adoptado prácticas de TQM. Se empleó un método mixto de estudios de caso y análisis comparativo de indicadores de desempeño antes y después de la implementación de TQM. Los hallazgos principales indican una reducción de defectos del 25 % y un aumento de la productividad del 18 %, lo que se traduce en ahorros de costos de hasta 15 % y una mejora del índice de lealtad del cliente en 12 puntos porcentuales. El estudio también identifica barreras como la resistencia al cambio y la necesidad de capacitación y liderazgo comprometido. Como aporte práctico al ciclo PHVA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act), se propone integrar la planificación estratégica de calidad en la fase “Plan”, ejecutar iniciativas de mejora continua en “Do”, medir defectos y satisfacción en “Check”, y retroalimentar los resultados para ajustar procesos en “Act”. Esta integración facilita una cultura organizacional orientada a la mejora permanente y al crecimiento sostenible.

Quality Improvement of the Forging Process Using Pareto Analysis and 8D Methodology in Automotive Manufacturing: A Case Study. Abstract: A systematic approach to nonconformity management and continuous improvements are the key elements of the quality management system. The objective of this paper is to present quality improvement for a manufacturing company producing forgings through the combination of several statistical methods and quality control techniques. First, Pareto analysis was applied, followed by the 8D (eight disciplines) methodology using a structured eight-step approach to problem solving following the PDCA (plan-do-check-act) method. The aim was to identify the problem and discover the critical causes of failures in the management system that allowed the problem to occur, by modifying and combining appropriate quality management methods and tools. The paper introduces a case study considering the forging process in the production of gearboxes, where customer complaints were identified in the last year, demanding the need to eliminate failures. Using the mentioned methods, the root cause of the problem was identified and permanent corrective action was planned and implemented according to the recommendations of the 8D report, which made it possible to reduce the likelihood of a recurrence of this problem and increase customer satisfaction.

Global 8D comprises a problem-solving methodology that seeks to identify and eliminate root causes of failure after the fact. The Global 8D problem-solving methodology was originated by the US government following World War II as MIL-STD 1520 and was later adopted and improved upon by the Ford Motor Company. Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) attempts to anticipate and correct problems before they occur [2,3]. Global 8D deals with the modes and causes of failure after the fact. Once used, Global 8D results can help improve the quality of future FMEA of a product, process, or service [4]. Global 8D is a methodology to identify and eliminate the root causes of failure and then implement permanent corrective actions to prevent a recurrence. The method is also designed to evaluate the effectiveness of failure mechanism controls that allowed the problem to escape undetected in the first place [4,5]. The method is typically used within an organization, and its results can be presented to the customer as quality control [6,7].

Global 8D employs a gateway step (D0) followed by eight discipline steps (D1–D8) [3,9]. Gateway step discipline D0—Prepare for Global 8D. This step confirms that the Global 8D methodology is needed. Symptoms are documented, showing that a problem has occurred, and a formal assessment is performed to justify the deployment of the resources required to perform a team-based cross-disciplinary problem-solving effort. Immediate damage control is conducted in the form of emergency response actions to prevent further undesirable consequences. Discipline D1—Create an interdisciplinary problem-solving team. The problem-solving team should consist of individuals who have the knowledge, time, authority, and skills to solve the problem and follow through by implementing corrective actions. The team composition should be cross-functional and include representation from all areas that need to be involved in containing, analyzing, correcting, and preventing the problem at hand. The team might describe the problem as specific as possible, including such details as: who suffers if the problem goes unsolved; what is the cost of not solving the problem; when was the problem discovered, how was it found, where was it found, and by whom; a description of the failure mode and rate; and any metrics and measures relevant to the problem situation. Discipline D3—Contain the problem. In this discipline, the team focuses on containing the issue. Intermediate containment actions are developed and implemented. Measures are taken to protect customers from the problem until permanent corrective actions can be taken. For example, all production that has been potentially affected by the problem should be isolated for detailed inspection. Those defective products that have been shipped may need to be recalled, and the production of those still in the manufacturing facility should be placed on hold until the problem has been fixed. Discipline D4—Identify root causes and escape points. During the fourth discipline, the problem-solving team identifies all potential causes and gathers as much evidence as possible to reliably test each potential cause against the problem data. When a cause-and-effect relationship is established, a detailed description of how the cause led to the failure is formulated. At this point, an escape point is identified where the control mechanism broke down and allowed the problem to go undetected. The escape point is identified as the first control point following the root cause. This constitutes the earliest opportunity to expose the problem if the control point had been effective. Once all root causes and escape points have been identified, the team can generate possible alternatives for corrective action. Discipline D5—Develop permanent corrective actions (PCAs). Discussion The use of the 8D report in production logistics allows you to effectively analyze all aspects of the problem before concluding and to collect all critical data, whether about the problem or the proposed corrective measures/solutions. All members of the group involved in seeking remedial action are involved in resolving the problem. It is suitable for specific, manageable, and well-defined issues. The advantage is that it plans specific steps to implement and evaluate the recommended corrective action/solution successfully. The 8D methodology can be considered as a conventional method, but if we combine the 8D methodology with the five whys method and Pareto analysis (in this case), then we can consider this presented solution as synergized and innovative. Abstract A systematic approach to nonconformity management and continuous improvements are the key elements of the quality management system. The objective of this paper is to present quality improvement for a manufacturing company producing forgings through the combination of several statistical methods and quality control techniques. First, Pareto analysis was applied, followed by the 8D (eight disciplines) methodology using a structured eight-step approach to problem solving following the PDCA (plan-do-check-act) method. The aim was to identify the problem and discover the critical causes of failures in the management system that allowed the problem to occur, by modifying and combining appropriate quality management methods and tools. The paper introduces a case study considering the forging process in the production of gearboxes, where customer complaints were identified in the last year, demanding the need to eliminate failures.

Using the mentioned methods, the root cause of the problem was identified and permanent corrective action was planned and implemented according to the recommendations of the 8D report, which made it possible to reduce the likelihood of a recurrence of this problem and increase customer satisfaction. 1. Introduction Quality requirements have expanded to the point where quality management has become the decisive factor in company management. Implementing quality standards allows for the maintenance of one’s position in the market, the gain of a competitive advantage, and the ability to compete in the sector [1]. Global 8D comprises a problem-solving methodology that seeks to identify and eliminate root causes of failure after the fact. The Global 8D problem-solving methodology was originated by the US government following World War II as MIL-STD 1520 and was later adopted and improved upon by the Ford Motor Company. Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) attempts to anticipate and correct problems before they occur [2,3].

improved upon by the Ford Motor Company. Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) attempts to anticipate and correct problems before they occur [2,3]. Global 8D deals with the modes and causes of failure after the fact. Once used, Global 8D results can help improve the quality of future FMEA of a product, process, or service [4]. Global 8D is a methodology to identify and eliminate the root causes of failure and then implement permanent corrective actions to prevent a recurrence. The method is also designed to evaluate the effectiveness of failure mechanism controls that allowed the problem to escape undetected in the first place [4,5]. The method is typically used within an organization, and its results can be presented to the customer as quality control [6,7]. The output of the 8D method is an 8D report based on the multi-stage work of the entire team using effective methods and tools for quality management or improvement [8,9]. The primary objective of the 8D methodology is to implement and consolidate corrective actions in relation to the quality management system. It comprises eight stages that set out a procedure to follow an established pattern [3,7,9].

Discipline D1—Create an interdisciplinary problem-solving team. The problem-solving team should consist of individuals who have the knowledge, time, authority, and skills to solve the problem and follow through by implementing corrective actions. The team composition should be cross-functional and include representation from all areas that need to be involved in containing, analyzing, correcting, and preventing the problem at hand. Discipline D2—Define the problem. The team might describe the problem as specific as possible, including such details as: who suffers if the problem goes unsolved; what is the cost of not solving the problem; when was the problem discovered, how was it found, where was it found, and by whom; a description of the failure mode and rate; and any metrics and measures relevant to the problem situation. Discipline D3—Contain the problem. In this discipline, the team focuses on containing the issue. Intermediate containment actions are developed and implemented.

D3—Contain the problem. In this discipline, the team focuses on containing the issue. Intermediate containment actions are developed and implemented. Measures are taken to protect customers from the problem until permanent corrective actions can be taken. For example, all production that has been potentially affected by the problem should be isolated for detailed inspection. Those defective products that have been shipped may need to be recalled, and the production of those still in the manufacturing facility should be placed on hold until the problem has been fixed. The team needs to verify the effectiveness of these actions. Discipline D4—Identify root causes and escape points. During the fourth discipline, the problem-solving team identifies all potential causes and gathers as much evidence as possible to reliably test each potential cause against the problem data. When a cause-and-effect relationship is established, a detailed description of how the cause led to the failure is formulated. At this point, an escape point is identified where the control mechanism broke down and allowed the problem to go undetected.

The escape point is identified as the first control point following the root cause. This constitutes the earliest opportunity to expose the problem if the control point had been effective. Once all root causes and escape points have been identified, the team can generate possible alternatives for corrective action. Discipline D5—Develop permanent corrective actions (PCAs). Discipline D5 is concerned with choosing permanent corrective actions and documenting the rationale for each. The team confirms that the recommended PCAs will solve the problem and will not produce any negative consequences. The implementation of PCAs can require a preliminary evaluation and, in some cases, a small pilot study. During this step, PCAs must also address control issues posed by the escape point. Discussion The use of the 8D report in production logistics allows you to effectively analyze all aspects of the problem before concluding and to collect all critical data, whether about the problem or the proposed corrective measures/solutions. All members of the group involved in seeking remedial action are involved in resolving the problem. It is suitable for specific, manageable, and well-defined issues. The advantage is that it plans specific steps to implement and evaluate the recommended corrective action/solution successfully. The 8D methodology can be considered as a conventional method, but if we combine the 8D methodology with the five whys method and Pareto analysis (in this case), then we can consider this presented solution as synergized and innovative. Quality Improvement of the Forging Process Using Pareto Analysis and 8D Methodology in Automotive Manufacturing: A Case Study. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es demostrar cómo la combinación de análisis de Pareto y la metodología 8D (eight disciplines) mejora la calidad del proceso de forja en la fabricación de cajas de cambios para la industria automotriz. El caso se sitúa en una empresa de forja ubicada en Eslovaquia (sector automotriz), donde en el último año se registraron numerosas quejas de clientes. Primero se aplicó el análisis de Pareto para identificar los defectos más frecuentes, y luego se siguió el ciclo PDCA (plan‑do‑check‑act) mediante los ocho pasos del 8D para investigar causas raíz y diseñar acciones correctivas permanentes. Los resultados mostraron una reducción de partes defectuosas de 95 a 26, equivalente a un descenso del 76,63 % en defectos, y una caída de los fallos de la cinta vibratoria de 38 a 10, logrando un 74 % de éxito en esa categoría. Estas mejoras aumentaron la satisfacción del cliente y disminuyeron la probabilidad de recurrencia del problema. El aporte práctico consiste en integrar el análisis de Pareto como herramienta de diagnóstico dentro del paso “D4 – Definir y verificar la causa raíz” del 8D, y usar los pasos “D5 – Elegir y validar acciones correctivas” y “D6 – Implementar acciones” para cerrar el ciclo PHVA, proporcionando una guía estructurada para la gestión de no conformidades y la mejora continua en procesos de manufactura.

Root Cause Analysis of Quality Issues in Watch Manufacturing Using Ishikawa and Pareto Diagrams. Abstract: This article provides a structured analysis of quality control issues in watch manufacturing using two primary tools: the Ishikawa (Fishbone) Diagram and the Pareto Diagram. The purpose is to identify, categorize, and prioritize the root causes of timekeeping inaccuracies and other defects impacting customer satisfaction. These defects, ranging from assembly errors to material quality issues, were analyzed to understand where targeted interventions could yield the greatest impact. The methodology involved constructing an Ishikawa Diagram to categorize potential causes into six key areas: Material, Human, Machine, Method, Measurement, and Environment. This structured approach helped break down complex problems into manageable sections, facilitating root cause identification. Following this, a Pareto Diagram was employed to apply the 80/20 rule, revealing that a small number of high-frequency defects (assembly errors and material issues) were responsible for the majority of complaints. Main findings indicate that assembly errors, improper procedures, and low-quality materials (e.g., worn cords, unsuitable materials for environmental conditions) are the leading causes of defects. Improvements in these high-impact areas could address over 60% of the issues, enhancing product reliability and customer satisfaction. The originality of this research lies in its integration of two well-established quality control tools in watch manufacturing, an area where precision is critical. By combining the systematic breakdown of the Ishikawa Diagram with the prioritization offered by the Pareto Diagram, the study provides a focused approach to defect reduction in the precision-manufacturing industry. This dual-method approach can be widely applied to industries that require meticulous quality control, as it enables organizations to allocate resources effectively, concentrating on the most impactful areas for improvement.

Root Cause Analysis of Quality Issues in Watch Manufacturing Using Ishikawa and Pareto Diagrams. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es identificar, categorizar y priorizar las causas raíz (root causes) de defectos que afectan la precisión horaria y la satisfacción del cliente en la fabricación de relojes (watch manufacturing). El contexto se sitúa en la industria de relojería de alta precisión, donde los fallos de ensamblaje y la calidad de los materiales son críticos. Se empleó una metodología dual: primero se construyó un Diagrama de Ishikawa (Fishbone Diagram) para dividir las causas potenciales en seis áreas (Material, Hombre, Máquina, Método, Medición y Medio ambiente); luego se aplicó un Diagrama de Pareto (Pareto Diagram) para implementar la regla 80/20 y determinar los defectos más frecuentes. Los hallazgos principales revelan que los errores de ensamblaje y los problemas de materiales representan más del 60 % de las quejas, confirmando que un pequeño número de defectos de alta frecuencia domina el panorama. Con base en estos resultados, se propone focalizar mejoras en los procesos de ensamblaje y en la selección de materiales, lo que permitiría reducir significativamente la tasa de defectos y cerrar el ciclo PHVA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act) al actuar primero sobre los factores de mayor impacto.

Integrating ISO 9001 and Industry 4.0. An implementation guideline and PDCA model for manufacturing sector. Abstract: The main purpose of this paper is to develop an implementation guideline for manufacturing companies integrating ISO 9001 requirements and Industry 4.0 technologies. The implementation guideline follows the Plan-Do-Check-Act model of ISO 9001 standard. We interviewed 25 experts and observed the quality management documentation of seven European manufacturing companies. Results emerged using thematic content analysis and we gained further insights from interviewees, allowing us to propose suggestions garnered from the interviews. The guideline demonstrates how requirements can be integrated with Industry 4.0 technologies such as radiofrequency identification tags, smart sensors, the internet of things, smart human interface, enterprise resource planning modules, artificial intelligence to improve a typical ISO 9001 quality management system. Some issues emerged relating to the fear of losing jobs, validation of quality control equipment based on artificial intelligence, and decision-making and problem-solving processes. The implications of this research are mainly related to the opening of a new debate concerning the integration between ISO 9001 and Industry 4.0 as well as the proposal, to our knowledge, of the first tentative integration. Manufacturing companies can use the guideline for integrating their quality management system with Industry 4.0 technologies while considering also the practical suggestions provided by the experts.

Integrating ISO 9001 and Industry 4.0. An implementation guideline and PDCA model for manufacturing sector. Resumen en español: El objetivo del estudio es diseñar una guía de implementación que permita a empresas manufactureras integrar los requisitos de ISO 9001 con tecnologías de Industry 4.0, estructurada bajo el modelo PDCA (Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act). El contexto se sitúa en el sector manufacturero europeo, analizando la documentación de calidad de siete compañías y realizando entrevistas a 25 expertos del área. El método combina observación documental y entrevistas semiestructuradas, analizadas mediante análisis de contenido temático. Los hallazgos principales indican que la integración es viable mediante RFID (etiquetas de identificación por radiofrecuencia), sensores inteligentes, IoT (Internet of Things), interfaces humano‑máquina, módulos ERP y IA (inteligencia artificial), aunque se detectan resistencias relacionadas con el temor a la pérdida de empleo y la validación de equipos de control basados en IA. La guía propuesta ofrece pasos concretos para cada fase del ciclo PDCA, facilitando la incorporación de estas tecnologías y proporcionando recomendaciones prácticas extraídas de los expertos. Como aporte práctico, la herramienta permite a las empresas planificar, ejecutar, verificar y ajustar su Sistema de Gestión de Calidad (SGC) de forma alineada con Industry 4.0, impulsando mejoras en la trazabilidad, la toma de decisiones y la resolución de problemas.

Empirical investigation of drivers, motivations and barriers for implementation of integrated continuous improvement system: a case of Ethiopian manufacturing industries. Abstract: Purpose Continuous improvement in an integrated approach is a philosophy developed over decades based on a set of management practices. It comprises enhancement methodologies that escalate success as well as diminishes letdowns. The state-of-the-art literature finds a variety of practices for the execution of continuous improvement (CI) system. However, it is rare to find an empirical study with an inclusive system that considers various practices in one frame for improving competitiveness. With this outlook, therefore, this study aims originally to identify drivers, motivations and barriers for the application of integrated CI system, and then conduct an empirical investigation within the context of Ethiopian manufacturing industries. Design/methodology/approach Justification of the problem, extensive review of literature, identification of practices, developing research framework, investigational analysis of the empirical study using reliability and descriptive statistical analysis and identifying leading drivers (unique practices and common factors), motivations and barriers are the research approaches used in this study. Furthermore, the primary data were collected through a self-administered questionnaire and were analyzed using a statistical package for social science (SPSS) 23 and the findings were triangulated to relate to the existing state-of-the-art literature. Findings The findings indicate 17 common factors associated with human, strategic, operational, technology, structure, resource and information factors; 21 unique practices of just-in-time (JIT), lean-six sigma (LSS), supply chain management (SCM), total productive maintenance (TPM), and total quality management (TQM) methodologies; 20 barriers connected with internal and external issues and 17 motivations linked to operational, innovation and business results are identified. In general, the empirical analysis discovers the practices are noteworthy and commonly supported by a least of 52% of the respondents. As a result, the first five prominent common factors, barriers, unique practices and motivations are also supported by a minimum of 72%, 73.9%, 65.8% and 75% of the respondents, respectively. Research limitations/implications Even though this is the first-ever study in the Ethiopian manufacturing sector with the focus on integrated CI practices of JIT, TQM, TPM, SCM and LSS initiatives, some limitations have existed and the major limitations of the study are, targeted merely small number manufacturing companies despite the fact that there are hundreds of companies implementing CI system in Ethiopia, and the data collected were only based on the perception of the respondents, and other information’s like annual reports was not employed to support the findings. Practical implications The findings of this study underlined that the implementation of drivers in relation to common factors and unique practices supported by exterminating barriers in manufacturing industries of Ethiopia enables to enhance competitiveness through attaining operational, innovation and business results though it requires a practical case application to prove this perception-based analysis. Originality/value Though there are a number of studies published on integrated continuous improvement, currently it is found that there is no literature focused on the identification and empirical investigation of drivers (common factors and unique practices), motivations and barriers for application of integrated CI system with the focus of JIT, TQM, TPM, SCM and LSS initiatives. Therefore, this is the first-ever study, and the empirical analysis of the study discovered that identified practices are providing valuable insights for manufacturing industries which will be on board on this voyage including institutions, practitioners and other sectors.
